relationship: related warning against desire awakened by beauty
rationale: The elders see Susanna's beauty and desire her. Proverbs warns against being overcome by desire for beauty and being hunted by one's own eyes; the connection concerns the observers' desire and does not attribute enticement to Susanna.

relationship: related rejection of divine awareness and disordered thinking

relationship: same-chapter disclosure of previously concealed desire
rationale: One elder questions the other about his early arrival, and each confesses his anguish. The earlier unit had expressly said neither admitted his desire to the other, providing the specific concealment that this conversation ends.

rationale: Susanna says compliance means death and refusal will not let her escape the elders' hands. Her next statement chooses falling into their hands without doing the act rather than sinning before the Lord, expressly resolving the dilemma she has just stated.

relationship: parallel refusal of sexual wrongdoing as sin before God

rationale: The lawless men plot to kill Susanna and approach the city's assembly. Proverbs warns against agreeing with ungodly men who invite participation in bloodshed and the unjust burial of a righteous man; the common collusion does not make the target's robbery scheme identical to the judicial plot.

rationale: The men order Susanna uncovered to satisfy their desire for her beauty. Matthew condemns looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her, identifying the intention of the gaze rather than treating Susanna as a consenting participant.

target_units.text: But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

relationship: shared laying of hands on the accused person's head
rationale: The elders and judges lay their hands on Susanna's head. Leviticus likewise commands those who heard a curse to lay hands on the offender's head before execution, providing a particular judicial gesture without making Susanna guilty or substituting that law's stoning for this narrative.

target_units.text: Daniel took thirty minas of pitch, together with fat and hair, boiled them together, made a cake, and threw it into the dragon’s mouth. It ate and burst apart. He showed it to the king, saying, “Are these not the things you revere, O king?”

relationship: same-chapter execution of the promised method without iron or a rod
rationale: Daniel uses a cake made from thirty minas of pitch with fat and hair; the dragon eats it and bursts apart. His earlier proposal had promised to kill it without iron or a rod, specifying the claim that this method demonstrates.
source_text: Daniel took thirty minas of pitch, together with fat and hair, boiled them together, made a cake, and threw it into the dragon’s mouth. It ate and burst apart. He showed it to the king, saying, “Are these not the things you revere, O king?”

target_units.text: Daniel said, “O king, give me authority, and I will kill the dragon without iron or a rod.”

relationship: related public backlash against a challenge to a local cult
rationale: The country's people gather against Daniel after Bel's destruction and the dragon's death. Acts likewise describes a furious crowd after complaints that Paul denies handmade objects are gods, with the additional threat to Artemis's temple and the craftsmen's trade; the cults and attacked persons are distinct.
source_text: All the people from the country gathered against Daniel and said, “The king has become a Jew! He has destroyed Bel and killed the dragon.”

target_units.text: You see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that things made by hands are not gods.

There is danger not only that this trade of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be reckoned as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the inhabited world worship will be stripped of her magnificence.”
When they heard this, they became full of rage and cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who traveled with Paul.

relationship: related capitulation to a hostile crowd
rationale: The king sees the crowd gathered against him and hands Daniel over to destruction. Luke likewise says the crowd's voices prevailed, Pilate granted their demand and handed Jesus over to their will, comparing the ruler's yielding without identifying the narratives or punishments.
source_text: The king saw that the crowd of the country had gathered against him. He called his companions and said, “I hand Daniel over to destruction.”

target_units.text: But they pressed him with loud voices, demanding that He be crucified, and their voices prevailed.
And Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, whom they were demanding; but he handed Jesus over to their will.

relationship: literary parallel of Daniel cast into a lions' pit
rationale: The crowds cast Daniel into a pit with seven lions, where he remains six days. Daniel 6 likewise places Daniel in a lions' pit, but describes its sealing and the king's overnight fast while God shuts the lions' mouths; its circumstances and duration are not substituted for Bel's.
source_text: There was a pit in which seven lions were kept. Those who plotted against the king were handed over to them, and each day two bodies of people condemned to death were supplied to them. The crowds threw Daniel into that pit so that he would be devoured and would not even receive burial. Daniel was in the pit for six days.

target_units.text: Then Daniel was thrown into the lions’ pit. A stone was brought and placed at the pit’s mouth, and the king sealed it with his own ring and his magnates’ rings, so that Daniel could not be taken away from them, nor could the king pull him up from the pit.
Then the king returned to his royal residence and spent the night fasting, grieving over Daniel. Daniel’s God, taking care of him, shut the lions’ mouths, and they did not trouble Daniel.

relationship: same-chapter redirection of the meal intended for reapers
rationale: Habakkuk has bread with stew and mixed wine and is going to the field's reapers. The angel's following command instead sends the meal he has to Daniel in Babylon's lions' pit, expressly changing the intended destination of that particular food.
source_text: On the sixth day, Habakkuk had bread crumbled in a trough with stew, and a jar of mixed wine. He was going into the field to the reapers.

target_units.text: An angel of the Lord spoke to Habakkuk, saying, “Thus says the Lord God to you: ‘Take the meal you have to Daniel in the lions’ pit in Babylon.’”

relationship: related divine direction to provide food for a servant
rationale: The angel relays God's command that Habakkuk take his meal to Daniel in the lions' pit. In Kings the Lord likewise directs provision for Elijah at the Chorrath wadi, commanding ravens to sustain him with bread and meat; the delivery agents and settings differ.
source_text: An angel of the Lord spoke to Habakkuk, saying, “Thus says the Lord God to you: ‘Take the meal you have to Daniel in the lions’ pit in Babylon.’”

target_units.text: The Lord’s word came to Elijah:
“Go from here eastward and hide yourself at the Chorrath wadi, which faces the Jordan.
You will drink water from the wadi, and I will command the ravens to sustain you there.”
Elijah acted according to the Lord’s word and stayed at the Chorrath wadi facing the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the wadi.

relationship: same-chapter lack of geographical knowledge answered by angelic transport
rationale: Habakkuk says he has not seen Babylon and does not know the pit's location. The next unit has the angel take him by his head's hair and set him above the pit, providing the story's specific solution to the obstacle he states.
source_text: Habakkuk said, “Lord God, I have not seen Babylon, and I do not know where the pit is.”

target_units.text: The angel of the Lord took Habakkuk by the hair of his head and set him above the pit in Babylon.

relationship: related extraordinary transport involving a person's head
rationale: The angel takes Habakkuk by the hair of his head and sets him above Babylon's pit. Ezekiel likewise describes lifting by the crown of the head, followed by a spirit's transport to Jerusalem in a vision of God; the source's hair and angel are not inserted into Ezekiel's supplied wording.
source_text: The angel of the Lord took Habakkuk by the hair of his head and set him above the pit in Babylon.

target_units.text: He stretched out the likeness of a hand and lifted me by the crown of my head. A spirit lifted me between earth and heaven and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, to the entrance of the inner gate facing north, where the pillar of the one acquiring stood.

relationship: parallel invitation to rise and eat a divinely provided meal
rationale: Habakkuk tells Daniel to get up and eat the meal sent by the Lord God. Kings likewise gives Elijah the invitation to rise and eat, repeated by the Lord's angel, there with a spelt cake and water rather than Habakkuk's meal.
source_text: Habakkuk said to Daniel, “Get up and eat the meal that the Lord God has sent you.”

target_units.text: He lay down and slept there under a plant. Behold, someone touched him and said to him, “Rise and eat.”
Elijah looked, and there at his head were a hearth cake of spelt and a flask of water. He rose, ate, and drank, then lay down again.
The Lord’s angel returned a second time, touched him, and said to him, “Rise, eat, for the journey is too much for you.”

relationship: shared divine care for those who love the Lord
rationale: Daniel declares that the Lord has remembered him and does not abandon those who love Him. The psalm likewise says the Lord guards all who love Him, while additionally contrasting their protection with the destruction of sinners.
source_text: Daniel said, “For the Lord God has remembered me, He who does not abandon those who love Him.”

target_units.text: The Lord guards all who love Him, and all sinners He will utterly destroy.

relationship: related extraordinary relocation after an appointed service
rationale: After Daniel eats, the angel returns Habakkuk to his original place on the same day. Acts likewise describes the Spirit snatching Philip away after baptism and Philip being found at Azotus; the agent, destination and explicit return are different.
source_text: Daniel ate. The angel of the Lord returned Habakkuk to the place from which he had taken him on that same day. And the Lord God remembered Daniel.

target_units.text: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
Philip was found at Azotus, and as he passed through, he proclaimed the good news in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

relationship: literary parallel of a king visiting the pit and finding Daniel alive
rationale: The mourning king bends toward the pit and sees Daniel sitting there. Daniel 6 likewise has Darius visit the pit weeping, ask whether Daniel lives and receive his answer that he is alive; the source's king is unnamed and its six-day setting remains distinct.
source_text: After these things the king went out mourning Daniel. He bent down into the pit and saw him sitting there.

target_units.text: King Darius rose early in the morning, took the satraps with him, and went and stood at the mouth of the lions’ pit.

Then the king called to Daniel with a loud voice and weeping: “O Daniel, are you perhaps alive? Has your God, whom you worship continually, saved you from the lions, so that they have not destroyed you?”
Then Daniel answered with a loud voice and said, “O king, I am still alive,

and God has saved me from the lions, because righteousness was found in me before Him. Before you also, O king, neither ignorant fault nor sin was found in me. Yet you listened to men who mislead kings and threw me into the lions’ pit for destruction.”
Then all the forces assembled and saw Daniel, whom the lions had not troubled.

relationship: shared confession that the Lord is God with none beside Him
rationale: The king declares the Lord God great and says no other exists besides Him. Deuteronomy likewise gives knowledge that the Lord is God and none is beside Him, there following Israel's account of divine acts rather than this king's discovery at the pit.
source_text: The king cried aloud and said, “The Lord God is great, and there is no other besides Him.”

target_units.text: That you might know that the Lord your God, He is God, and there is none beside Him.

relationship: literary parallel of Daniel's opponents being given to the lions
rationale: The king brings Daniel out and throws those responsible for his destruction into the pit, where they are devoured. Daniel 6 likewise gives the two men who testified against Daniel to the lions, additionally naming their wives and children and crushed bones; the target unit does not itself repeat Daniel's removal.
source_text: The king brought Daniel out of the pit. Before Daniel’s eyes he threw into the pit those responsible for his destruction, and they were devoured.

target_units.text: Then those two men who had testified against Daniel, with their wives and children, were thrown to the lions. The lions killed them and crushed their bones.
